name: Strato of Sardis
dates: probably the reign of Hadrian, 2nd century AD (Paton’s date)
bio: Strato, usually called Strato of Sardis, is the poet whose name gives its title to Book XII of the Greek Anthology, the Musa Puerilis, a collection of epigrams on the love of boys. In his introduction to that book Paton judges that Strato lived probably in the reign of Hadrian, and that it was a Byzantine compiler, perhaps Cephalas, who inserted into the book the many poems of Meleager and other earlier poets.

poems.title: Book XI, 19
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Drink and love now, Damocrates, for we shall not drink for ever or be for ever with the lads. Let us bind our heads with garlands and scent ourselves before others bear flowers and scent to our tombs. Now may my bones inside me drink all the more wine, and when they are dead let Deucalion’s flood cover them.

poems.title: Book XI, 21
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Agathon’s lizard was rosy-fingered the other day ; now it is already even rosy-armed.

poems.title: Book XI, 117
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: The physician Capito anointed Chryses’ eyes then when he could see a high tower from a mile off and aman from a furlong and a quail from ten yards and a louse even from a foot. Now from a furlong he cannot see the town and from two hundred feet cannot see that the lighthouse is alight ; he scarcely sees a horse from half a foot off and as for the quail he once saw, he can’t even see a large ostrich. If he manages to give him another dose, he won’t ever after be able to see even an elephant standing close to him.

poems.title: Book XII, 1
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: “Let us begin from Zeus,’ as Aratus said, and you, O Muses, I trouble not to-day. For if I love boys and associate with boys, what is that to the Muses of Helicon?

poems.title: Book XII, 2
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Look not in my pages for Priam by the altar, nor for the woes of Medea and Niobe, nor for Itys in his chamber and the nightingales amid the leaves; for earlier poets wrote of all these things in profusion. But look for sweet Love mingled with the jolly Graces, and for Bacchus. No grave face suits them.

poems.title: Book XII, 4
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I delight in the prime of a boy of twelve, but one of thirteen is much more desirable. He who is fourteen is a still sweeter flower of the Loves, and one who is just beginning his fifteenth year is yet more delightful. The sixteenth year is that of the gods, and as for the seventeenth it is not for me, but for Zeus, to seek it. But if one has a desire for those still older, he no longer plays, but now seeks “ And answering him back.”

poems.title: Book XII, 5
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I like them pale, and I also love those with a skin the colour of honey, and the fair too; and on the other hand I am taken by the black-haired. Nor do I dismiss brown eyes; but above all I love sparkling black eyes.

poems.title: Book XII, 8
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Just now, as I was passing the place where they make garlands, I saw a boy interweaving flowers with a bunch of berries. Nor did I pass by unwounded, but standing by him I said quietly, “For how much will you sell me your garland?” He grew redder than his roses, and turning down his head said, “Go right away in case my father sees you.” I bought some wreaths as a pretence, and when I reached home crowned the gods, beseeching them to grant me him.

poems.title: Book XII, 9
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Now thou art fair, Diodorus, and ripe for lovers, but even if thou dost marry, we shall not abandon thee.

poems.title: Book XII, 10
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Even though the invading down and the delicate auburn curls of thy temples have leapt upon thee, that does not make me shun my beloved, but his beauty is mine, even if there be a beard and hairs.

poems.title: Book XII, 11
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Yesterday I had Philostratus for the night, but was incapable, though he (how shall I say it?) was quite complaisant. No longer, my friends, count me your friend, but throw me off a tower as I have become too much of an Astyanax.

poems.title: Book XII, 13
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I once found some beardless doctors, not prone to love, grinding a natural antidote for it. They, on being surprised, besought me to keep it quiet, and I said, “I am mum, but you must cure me.”

poems.title: Book XII, 15
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If a plank pinched Graphicus in the bath, what will become of me, a man? Even wood feels.

poems.title: Book XII, 16
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Seek not to hide our love, Philocrates; the god himself without that hath sufficient power to trample on my heart. But give me a taste of a blithe kiss. The time shall come when thou shalt beg such favour from others.

poems.title: Book XII, 21
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: How long shall we steal kisses and covertly signal to each other with chary eyes? How long shall we talk without coming to a conclusion, linking again and again idle deferment to deferment? If we tarry we shall waste the good; but before the envious ones come, Phidon, let us add deeds to words.

poems.title: Book XII, 175
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Either be not jealous with your friends about your slave boys, or do not provide girlish-looking cup-bearers. For who is of adamant against love, or who succumbs not to wine, and who does not look curiously at pretty boys? This is the way of living men, but if you like, Diophon, go away to some place where there is no love and no drunkenness, and there induce Tiresias or Tantalus to drink with you, the one to see nothing and the other only to see.

poems.title: Book XII, 176
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Way are you draped down to your ankles in that melancholy fashion, Menippus, you who used to tuck up your dress to your thighs? Or why do you pass me by with downcast eyes and without a word? I know what you are hiding from me. They have come, those things I told you would come.

poems.title: Book XII, 177
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Last evening Moeris, at the hour when we bid good night, embraced me, I know not whether in reality or in a dream. I remember now quite accurately everything else, what he said to me and the questions he asked, but whether he kissed me too or not I am at a loss to know; for if it be true, how is it that I, who then became a god, am walking about on earth ?

poems.title: Book XII, 178
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I caught fire when Theudis shone among the other boys, like the sun that rises on the stars. Therefore I am still burning now, when the down of night overtakes him, for though he be setting, yet he is still the sun.

poems.title: Book XII, 179
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I swore to thee, son of Gronos, that never, not even to myself, would I utter what Theudis told me I might have. But my froward soul flies high in exultation and cannot contain the good. But I will out with it: pardon me, Zeus, “ He yielded.” Father Zeus, what delight is there in good fortune that is known to none?

poems.title: Book XII, 180
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I see some burning heat; but cease, boy, from waving in the air near me the napkin of fine linen. I have another fire within me lit by the wine thou didst serve, and aroused more with thy fanning.

poems.title: Book XII, 181
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: It is a lying fable, Theocles, that the Graces are good and that there are three of them in Orchomenus; for five times ten dance round thy face, all archers, ravishers of other men’s souls.

poems.title: Book XII, 182
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Now thou givest me these futile kisses, when the fire of love is quenched, when not even apart from it do I regard thee as a sweet friend. For I remember those days of thy stubborn resistance. Yet even now, Daphnis, though it be late, let repentance find its place.

poems.title: Book XII, 183
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: What delight, Heliodorus, is there in kisses, if thou dost not kiss me, pressing against me with greedy lips, but on the tips of mine with thine closed and motionless, as a wax image at home kisses me even without thee.

poems.title: Book XII, 184
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Study not to capture Menedemus by craft, but sign to him with your eyebrows and he will say openly, “ Go on, I follow.” For there is no delay, and he even “outrunneth him who guides him,’ and is more expeditious not than a water-channel but than a river.

poems.title: Book XII, 185
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: These airified boys, with their purple-edged robes, whom we cannot get at, Diphilus, are like ripe figs on high crags, which the vultures and ravens eat.

poems.title: Book XII, 186
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: How long, Mentor, shalt thou maintain this arrogant brow, not even bidding “good day,” as if thou shouldst keep young for all time or tread for ever the pyrrhic dance? Look forward and consider thy end too. Thy beard will come, the last of evils but the greatest, and then thou shalt know what scarcity of friends is.

poems.title: Book XII, 187
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: How, Dionysius, shall you teach a boy to read when you do not even know how to make the transition from one note to another? You have passed so quickly from the highest note to a deep one, from the slightest rise to the most voluminous. Yet I bear you no grudge; only study, and striking both say Lambda and Alpha to the envious.

poems.title: Book XII, 188
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If I do you a wrong by kissing you, and you think this an injury, kiss me too, inflicting the same on me as a punishment.

poems.title: Book XII, 189
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Who crowned all thy head with roses? If it was a lover, blessed is he, but if it was thy father, he too has eyes.

poems.title: Book XII, 190
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Blest is he who painted thee, and blest is this wax that knew how to be conquered by thy beauty. Would I could become a creeping wood-worm that I might leap up and devour this wood.

poems.title: Book XII, 191
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Wast thou not yesterday a boy, and we had never even dreamt of this beard coming? How did this accursed thing spring up, covering with hair all that was so pretty before? Heavens what a marvel! Yesterday you were Troilus and to-day how have you become Priam?

poems.title: Book XII, 192
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I am not charmed by long hair and needless ringlets taught in the school of Art, not of Nature, but by the dusty grime of a boy fresh from the play-ground and the colour given to the limbs by the gloss of oil. My love is sweet when unadorned, but a fraudulent beauty has in it the work of female Cypris.

poems.title: Book XII, 193
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Thou dost not even take to heart, Artemidorus, what the Avenging Goddesses of Smyrna say to thee, “ Nothing beyond due measure,” but thou art always acting, talking loud in a tone so arrogant and savage, not even becoming in an actor. Thou shalt remember all this, haughty boy; thou, too, shalt love and play the part of “The barred-out lady.”

poems.title: Book XII, 194
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If Zeus still carried off mortal boys from earth to the sky to be ministrants of the sweet nectar, an eagle would ere this have borne my lovely Agrippa on his wings to the service of the immortals. For yea, by thyself I swear it, Son of Cronos, Father of the world, if thou lookest on him thou wilt at once find fault with the Phrygian boy of the house of Dardanus.

poems.title: Book XII, 195
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: The meads that love the Zephyr are not abloom with so many flowers, the crowded splendour of the spring-tide, as are the high-born boys thou shalt see, Dionysius, all moulded by Cypris and the Graces. And chief among them, look, flowers Milesius, like a rose shining with its sweet-scented petals. But perchance he knows not, that as a lovely flower is killed by the heat, so is beauty by a hair.

poems.title: Book XII, 196
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Thy eyes are sparks, Lycinus, divinely fair; or rather, master mine, they are rays that shoot forth flame. Even for a little season I cannot look at thee face to face, so bright is the lightning from both.

poems.title: Book XII, 197
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: “Know the time” said one of the seven sages; for all things, Philippus, are more loveable when in their prime. A cucumber, too, is a fruit we honour at first when we see it in its garden bed, but after, when it ripens, it is food for swine.

poems.title: Book XII, 198
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I am a friend of youth and prefer not one boy to another, judging them by their beauty; for one has one charm, another another.

poems.title: Book XII, 199
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I have drunk already in sufficient measure, for both my mind’s and my tongue’s steadiness is relaxed. The flame of the lamp is torn into two, and I count the guests double, though I try over and over again. And now not only am I in a flutter for the wine-pourer, but I look, out of season, at the Water-pourer too.

poems.title: Book XII, 200
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I hate resistance to my embrace when I kiss, and pugnacious cries, and violent opposition with the hands, but at the same time I have no great desire for him who, when he is in my arms, is at once ready and abandons himself effusively. I wish for one half-way between the two, such as is he who knows both how to give himself and how not to give himself.

poems.title: Book XII, 201
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If Cleonicus does not come now I will never receive him in my house, by —. I will not swear; for if he did not come owing to a dream he had, and then does appear to-morrow, it is not all over with me because of the loss of this one day.

poems.title: Book XII, 202
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Winged Love bore me through the air, Damis, when I saw your letter which told me you had arrived here; and swiftly I flew from Smyrna to Sardis; if Zetes or Calais had been racing me they would have been left behind.

poems.title: Book XII, 203
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: You kiss me when I don’t wish it, and you don’t wish it when I kiss you; when I fly you are facile, when I attack you are difficult.

poems.title: Book XII, 204
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Now you may say, “Golden gifts for brazen.” Sosiades the fair and Diocles the bushy are playing at “Give and take.’ Who compares roses with brambles, or figs with toadstools? Who compares a lamb like curdled milk with an ox? What dost thou give, thoughtless boy, and what dost thou receive in return? Such gifts did Diomede give to Glaucus.

poems.title: Book XII, 205
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: My neighbour’s quite tender young boy provokes me not a little, and laughs in no novice manner to show me that he is willing. But he is not more than twelve years old. Now the unripe grapes are unguarded; when he ripens there will be watchmen and stakes.

poems.title: Book XII, 206
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: A. “If you are minded to do thus, take your adversary by the middle, and laying him down get astride of him, and shoving forward, fall on him and hold him tight.” B. “You are not in your right senses, Diophantus. I am only just capable of doing this, but boys’ wrestling is different. Fix yourself fast and stand firm, Cyris, and support it when I close with you. He should learn to practise with a fellow before learning to practise himself.”

poems.title: Book XII, 207
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Yesterday Diocles in the bath brought up a lizard from the tub, “ Aphrodite rising from the waves.” If someone had shown it to Paris then in Ida, he would have pronounced the three goddesses to be less fair than it.

poems.title: Book XII, 208
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Happy little book,’ I grudge it thee not; some boy reading thee will rub thee, holding thee under his chin, or press thee against his delicate lips, or will roll thee up resting on his tender thighs, O most blessed of books. Often shalt thou betake thee into his bosom, or, tossed down on his chair, shalt dare to touch without fear, and thou shalt talk much before him all alone with him; but I supplicate thee, little book, speak something not unoften on my behalf.

poems.title: Book XII, 209
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Lie not by me with so sour a face and so dejected, Diphilus, and be not a boy of the common herd. Put a little wantonness into your kisses and the preliminaries, toying, touching, scratching, your look and your words.

poems.title: Book XII, 211
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If you were still uninitiated in the matter about which I go on trying to persuade you, you would be right in being afraid, thinking it is perhaps something formidable. But if your master’s bed has made you proficient in it, why do you grudge granting the favour to another, receiving the same? For he, after summoning you to the business, dismisses you, and being your lord and master, goes to sleep without even addressing a word to you. But here you will have other enjoyments, playing on equal terms, talking together, and all else by invitation and not by order.

poems.title: Book XII, 212
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Woe is me! Why in tears again and so woebegone, my lad? Tell me plainly; don’t give me pain ; what do you want? You hold out the hollow of your hand to me. Iam done for! You are begging perhaps for payment; and where did you learn that? You no longer love slices of seed-cake and sweet sesame, and nuts to play at shots with, but already your mind is set on gain. May he who taught you perish! What a boy of mine he has spoilt !

poems.title: Book XII, 213
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: You rest your splendid loins against the wall, Cyris. Why do you tempt the stone? It is incapable.

poems.title: Book XII, 214
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Grant it me and take the coin. You will say “I am rich.” Then, like a king, make me a present of the favour.

poems.title: Book XII, 215
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Now thou art spring, and afterward summer, and next what shalt thou be, Cyris? Consider, for thou shalt be dry stubble too.

poems.title: Book XII, 217
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: So soon thou rushest to the wars, still an ignorant boy and delicate. What art thou doing? Ho look to it, change thy resolve. Alas who persuaded thee to grasp the spear? Who bad thee take the shield in thy hand or hide that head in a helmet? Most blessed he, whoe’er he be, who, some new Achilles, shall take his pleasure in the tent with such a Patroclus !

poems.title: Book XII, 218
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: How long shall I bear with thee, thus laughing only and never uttering a word? Tell me this plainly, Pasiphilus. I entreat and thou laughest ; I entreat again and no answer; I weep and thou laughest. Cruel boy, is this a laughing matter?

poems.title: Book XII, 219
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: You want payment too, you schoolmasters! How ungrateful you are! For why? Is it a smal thing to look on boys and speak to them, and kiss them when you greet them? Is not this alone worth a hundred pounds? If anyone has good-looking boys, let him send them to me and let them kiss me, and receive whatever payment they wish from me.

poems.title: Book XII, 220
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Thou art not in fetters for stealing the fire, ill-advised Prometheus, but because thou didst spoil the clay of Zeus. In moulding men thou didst add hairs, and hence comes the horrible beard, and hence boys’ legs grow rough. For this thou art devoured by Zeus’ eagle, which carried off Ganymede ; for the beard is a torment to Zeus, too.

poems.title: Book XII, 221
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Hie thee to holy Heaven, eagle ; away, bearing the boy, thy twin wings outspread. Go, holding tender Ganymede, and let him not drop, the ministrant of Zeus’ sweetest cups. And take heed not to make the boy bleed with the crooked claws of thy feet, lest Zeus, sore aggrieved thereby, suffer pain.

poems.title: Book XII, 223
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: His face as he approaches seems altogether delightful to me, and that suffices, and I turn not my head to look at him again as he passes. For thus do we look at the statue of a god and a temple, in front, but need not look at the back chamber too.

poems.title: Book XII, 224
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: We walk together in a good path, Diphilus, and take thou thought how it shall continue to be even as it was from the beginning. To the lot of each has fallen a winged thing; for in thee is beauty and in me love; but both are fugitive. Now they remain in unison for a season, but if they do not guard one another they take wing and are gone.

poems.title: Book XII, 226
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: All night long, my dripping eyes tear-stained, I strive to rest my spirit that grief keeps awake— grief for this separation from my friend since yesterday, when Theodorus, leaving me here alone, went to his own Ephesus. If he come not back soon I shall be no longer able to bear the solitude of my bed.

poems.title: Book XII, 227
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Even if I desire to avoid looking at a pretty boy when I meet him, I have scarcely passed him when I at once turn round.

poems.title: Book XII, 228
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: That an immature boy should do despite to his insensible age carries more disgrace to the friend who tempts him than to himself, and for a grown-up youth to submit to that, his season for which is past, is twice as disgraceful to him who consents as it is to his tempter. But there is a time, Moeris, when it is no longer unseemly in the one, and not yet so in the other, as is the case with you and me at present.

poems.title: Book XII, 229
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: What a good goddess is that Nemesis, to avert whom, dreading her as she treadeth behind us, we spit in our bosom! Thou didst not see her at thy heels, but didst think that for ever thou shouldst possess thy grudging beauty. Now it has perished utterly ; the very wrathful goddess has come, and we, thy servants, now pass thee by.

poems.title: Book XII, 231
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Eutychides, who is in love, has lost his father. Ah, the ever lucky fellow! His father used ever to be good-natured to him about anything he wished, and now is a benevolent corpse. But I must still play in secret. Alas for my evil fate and my father’s immortality !

poems.title: Book XII, 234
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If thou gloriest in thy beauty, know that the rose too blooms, but withers of a sudden and is cast away on the dunghill. ‘To blossom and to beauty the same time is allotted, and envious time withers both together.

poems.title: Book XII, 235
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If beauty grows old, give me of it ere it depart ; but if it remains with thee, why fear to give what shall remain thine?

poems.title: Book XII, 236
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: A certain eunuch has good-looking servant-boys— for what use?—and he does them abominable injury. Truly, like the dog in the manger with the roses, and stupidly barking, he neither gives the good thing to himself nor to anyone else.

poems.title: Book XII, 237
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Off with thee, pretended hater of evil; off with thee, low-minded boy, who didst swear so lately that never again wouldst thou grant me it. Swear no longer now ; for I know, and thou canst not conceal it from me, where it was, and how, and with whom, and for how much.

poems.title: Book XII, 239
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: You ask for five drachmas: I will give ten and you will... have twenty. Is a gold sovereign enough for you? Sovereign gold was enough for Danae.

poems.title: Book XII, 241
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: You have made a hook, my child, and I am the fish you have caught. Pull me where you will, but don’t run or you might lose me.

poems.title: Book XII, 244
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: If I see a white boy it is the death of me, and if it be a honey-complexioned one I am on fire; but if it be a flaxen-haired one I am utterly melted.

poems.title: Book XII, 246
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: A pair of brothers love me. I know not which of them I should decide to take for my master, for I love them both. One goes away from me and the other approaches. The best of the one is his presence, the best of the other my desire for him in his absence.

poems.title: Book XII, 247
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Theodorus, as once Idomeneus brought from Crete to Troy Meriones to be his squire, such a dexterous friend have I in thee; for Meriones was in some things his servant, in others his minion. And do thou, too, all day go about the business of my life, but at night, by Heaven, let us essay Meriones.

poems.title: Book XII, 248
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Who can tell if his beloved begins to pass his prime, if he is ever with him and never separated? Who that pleased yesterday can fail to please to-day, and if he please now, what can befall him to make him displease to-morrow ?

poems.title: Book XII, 249
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Ox-born bee, why, catching sight of my honey, dost thou fly across to the boy’s face, smooth as glass? Wilt thou not cease thy humming and thy effort to touch his most pure skin with thy flower-gathering feet? Off to thy honey-bearing hive, where’er it be, thou truant, lest I bite thee! I, too, have a sting, even love's.

poems.title: Book XII, 250
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Gone out in revel at night after supper, I, the wolf, found a lamb standing at the door, the son of my neighbour Aristodicus, and throwing my arms round him I kissed him to my heart’s content, promising on my oath many gifts. And now what present shall I bring to him? He does not deserve cheating or Italian perfidy.

poems.title: Book XII, 251
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Hitherto we had kisses face to face, and all that precedes the trial; for you were still a little boy, Diphilus. “But now I supplicate for them behind, that will be no longer with thee” afterwards; for let all things be as befits our age.

poems.title: Book XII, 252
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: I will burn thee, door, with the torch; and burning him who is within, too, in my drunken fury, I will straight depart a fugitive, and sailing over the purple Adriatic, shall, in my wanderings, at least lie in ambush at doors that open at night.

poems.title: Book XII, 253
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Give me thy right hand for a time, not to stop me from the dance, even though the fair boy made mockery of me. But if he had not been lying at the wrong time next his father, he would not, I swear, have seen me drunk to no purpose.

poems.title: Book XII, 254
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: From what temple, whence comes this band of Loves shedding radiance on all? Sirs, my eyes are dazed. Which of them are slaves, which freemen ? I cannot tell. Is their master a man? It is impossible; or if he be, he is much greater than Zeus, who only had Ganymede, though such a mighty god.

poems.title: Book XII, 255
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Unsociable man does not the word itself teach you by the words from which it is truly derived? Everyone is called a lover of boys, not a lover of big boys. Have you any retort to that? I preside over the Pythian games, you over the Olympian, and those whom I reject and remove from the list you receive as competitors.

poems.title: Book XII, 258
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text: Perchance someone in future years, listening to these trifles of mine, will think these pains of love were all my own. No! I ever scribble this and that for this and that boy-lover, since some god gave me this gift.

poems.title: The First Kiss (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: At evening, at the hour when we say good-night, Moeris kissed me, I know not whether really or in a dream; for very clearly I now have the rest in mind, all she said to me, and all that she asked me of; but whether she kissed me too, I doubt and guess; for if it is true, how, after being set in heaven, do I go to and fro upon earth?

poems.title: Love's Immortality (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Who may know if a loved one passes the prime, while ever with him and never left alone? who may not satisfy to-day who satisfied yesterday? and if he did satisfy, what should befall him not to satisfy to-morrow?

poems.title: Withered Blossoms (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If thou boast in thy beauty, know that the rose too blooms, but quickly being withered, is cast on the dunghill; for blossom and beauty have the same time allotted to them, and both together envious time withers away.

poems.title: Hoarded Beauty (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If beauty grows old, impart thou of it before it be gone; and if it abides, why fear to give away what thou dost keep?

poems.title: Prologue (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Seek not on my pages Priam at the altars nor Medea's and Niobe's woes, nor Itys in the hidden chambers, and the nightingales among the leaves; for of all these things former poets wrote abundantly; but mingling with the blithe Graces, sweet Love and the Wine-god; and grave looks become not them.

poems.title: Before the Deluge (Mackail)
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Drink now and love, Damocrates, since not for ever shall we drink nor for ever hold fast our delight; let us crown our heads with garlands and perfume ourselves, before others bring these offerings to our graves. Now rather let my bones drink wine inside me; when they are dead, let Deucalion's deluge sweep them away.

poems.title: The Kiss
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
It was at even and the hour in which good-nights are bid
That Mœris kissed me, if indeed I do not dream she did.
Of all the rest that happened there is naught that I forget,
No word she said, no question of all she asked,--and yet
If she indeed did kiss me, my doubt can not decide,
For how could I still walk the earth had I been deified!

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.177: ἑσπερίην Μοῖρίς με, καθʼ ἣν ὑγιαίνομεν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἑσπερίην Μοῖρίς με, καθʼ ἣν ὑγιαίνομεν ὥρην,
οὐκ οἶδʼ εἴτε σαφῶς, εἴτʼ ὄναρ, ἠσπάσατο.
ἤδη γὰρ τὰ μὲν ἄλλα μάλʼ ἀτρεκέως ἐνόησα,
χὠκόσα μοι προσέφη, χὠκόσ’ ἐπυνθάνετο
εἰ δέ με καὶ πεφίληκε τεκμαίρομαι· εἰ γὰρ ἀληθές,
πῶς ἀποθειωθεὶς πλάζομʼ ἐπιχθόνιος;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.248: τίς δύναται γνῶναι τὸν ἐρώμενον εἰ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.234: εἰ κάλλει καυχᾷ, γίνωσκʼ ὅτι καὶ ῥόδον
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ κάλλει καυχᾷ, γίνωσκʼ ὅτι καὶ ῥόδον ἀνθεῖ·
ἀλλὰ μαρανθὲν ἄφνω σὺν κοπρίοις ἐρίφη.
ἄνθος γὰρ καὶ κάλλος ἴσον χρόνον ἐστὶ λαχόντα·
ταῦτα δʼ ὁμῇ φθονέων ἐξεμάρανε χρόνος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.19: καὶ πίε νῦν καὶ ἔρα, Δαμόκρατες· οὐ γὰρ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
καὶ πίε νῦν καὶ ἔρα, Δαμόκρατες· οὐ γὰρ ἐς αἰεὶ
πιόμεθʼ, οὐδʼ αἰεὶ παισὶ συνεσσόμεθα.
καὶ στεφάνοις κεφαλὰς πυκασώμεθα, καὶ μυρίσωμεν
αὑτούς, πρὶν τύμβοις ταῦτα φέρειν ἑτέρους.
νῦν ἐν ἐμοὶ πιέτω μέθυ τὸ πλέον ὀστέα τἀμά·
νεκρὰ δὲ Δευκαλίων αὐτὰ κατακλυσάτω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.21: πρῴην τὴν σαύραν Ἀγάθων ῥοδοδάκτυλον
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
πρῴην τὴν σαύραν Ἀγάθων ῥοδοδάκτυλον εἶχεν
νῦν δʼ αὐτὴν ἤδη καὶ ῥοδόπηχυν ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XI.117: ἰητρὸς Καπίτων Χρύσην ἐνέχρισεν, ὁρῶντα
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἰητρὸς Καπίτων Χρύσην ἐνέχρισεν, ὁρῶντα
ὀκτὼ μὲν μακρὸν πύργον ἀπὸ σταδίων,
ἄνδρα δʼ ἀπὸ σταδίου, διὰ δώδεκα δʼ ὄρτυγα πηχῶν,
φθεῖρα δʼ ἀπὸ σπιθαμῶν καὶ δύο δερκόμενον.
νῦν δʼ ἀπὸ μὲν σταδίου πόλιν οὐ βλέπει, ἐκ δὲ διπλέθρου
καιόμενον κατιδεῖν τὸν φάρον οὐ δύναται·
ἵππον ἀπὸ σπιθαμῆς δὲ μόλις βλέπει, ἀντὶ δὲ τοῦ πρὶν
ὄρτυγος οὐδὲ μέγαν στρουθὸν ἰδεῖν δύναται.
ἂν δὲ προσεγχρίσας αὐτὸν φθάσῃ, οὐδʼ ἐλέφαντα
οὐκέτι μήποτʼ ἴδῃ πλησίον ἑσταότα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.1: ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, καθὼς εἴρηκεν Ἄρατος·
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα, καθὼς εἴρηκεν Ἄρατος·
ὑμῖν δʼ, ὦ Μοῦσαι, σήμερον οὐκ ἐνοχλῶ.
εἰ γὰρ ἐγὼ παῖδάς τε φιλῶ καὶ παισὶν ὁμιλῶ,
τοῦτο τί πρὸς Μούσας τὰς Ἑλικωνιάδας;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.2: μὴ ζήτει δέλτοισιν ἐμαῖς Πρίαμον παρὰ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
μὴ ζήτει δέλτοισιν ἐμαῖς Πρίαμον παρὰ βωμοῖς,
μηδὲ τὰ Μηδείης πένθεα καὶ Νιόβης,
μηδʼ Ἴτυν ἐν θαλάμοις, καὶ ἀηδόνας ἐν πετάλοισιν
ταῦτα γὰρ οἱ πρότεροι πάντα χύδην ἔγραφον·
ἀλλʼ ἱλαραῖς Χαρίτεσσι μεμιγμένον ἡδὺν Ἔρωτα,
καὶ Βρόμιον τούτοις δʼ ὀφρύες οὐκ ἔπρεπον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.4: ἀκμῇ δωδεκέτους ἐπιτέρπομαι· ἔστι δὲ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἀκμῇ δωδεκέτους ἐπιτέρπομαι· ἔστι δὲ τούτου
χὠ τρισκαιδεκέτης πουλὺ ποθεινότερος·
χὠ τὰ δὶς ἑπτὰ νέμων, γλυκερώτερον ἄνθος Ἐρώτων
τερπνότερος δʼ ὁ τρίτης πεντάδος ἀρχόμενος·
ἑξεπικαιδέκατον δὲ θεῶν ἔτος· ἑβδόματον δὲ
καὶ δέκατον ζητεῖν οὐκ ἐμόν, ἀλλὰ Διός.
εἰ δʼ ἐπὶ πρεσβυτέρους τις ἔχει πόθον, οὐκέτι παίζει,
ἀλλʼ ἤδη ζητεῖ τὸν δʼ ἀπαμειβόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.5: τοὺς λευκοὺς ἀγαπῶ, φιλέω δʼ ἅμα τοὺς
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
τοὺς λευκοὺς ἀγαπῶ, φιλέω δʼ ἅμα τοὺς μελιχρώδεις
καὶ ξανθούς, στέργω δʼ ἔμπαλι τοὺς μέλανας.
οὐδὲ κόρας ξανθὰς παραπέμπομαι· ἀλλὰ περισσῶς
τοὺς μελανοφθάλμους αἰγλοφανεῖς τε φιλῶ.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.8: εἶδον ἐγώ τινα παῖδα † ἐπανθοπλοκοῦντα
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἶδον ἐγώ τινα παῖδα † ἐπανθοπλοκοῦντα κόρυμβον,
ἄρτι παρερχόμενος τὰ στεφανηπλόκια·
οὐδʼ ἄτρωτα παρῆλθον· ἐπιστὰς δʼ ἥσυχος αὐτῷ
φημὶ πόσου πωλεῖς τὸν σὸν ἐμοὶ στέφανον;
μᾶλλον τῶν καλύκων δʼ ἐρυθαίνετο, καὶ κατακύψας
φησὶ μακρὰν χώρει, μή σε πατὴρ ἐσίδῃ.
ὠνοῦμαι προφάσει στεφάνους, καὶ οἴκαδʼ ἀπελθὼν
ἐστεφάνωσα θεούς, κεῖνον ἐπευξάμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.9: ἄρτι καλός, Διόδωρε, σύ, καὶ φιλέουσι
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἄρτι καλός, Διόδωρε, σύ, καὶ φιλέουσι πέπειρος·
ἀλλὰ καὶ ἢν γήμῃς, οὐκ ἀπολειψόμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.10: εἰ καί σοι τριχόφοιτος ἐπεσκίρτησεν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ καί σοι τριχόφοιτος ἐπεσκίρτησεν ἴουλος,
καὶ τρυφεραὶ κροτάφων ξανθοφυεῖς ἕλικες,
οὐδʼ οὕτω φεύγω τὸν ἐρώμενον ἀλλὰ τὸ κάλλος
τούτου, κἂν πώγων, κἂν τρίχες, ἡμέτερον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.11: ἐχθὲς ἔχων ἀνὰ νύκτα Φιλόστρατον, οὐκ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἐχθὲς ἔχων ἀνὰ νύκτα Φιλόστρατον, οὐκ ἐδυνήθην,
κείνου, πῶς εἴπω; πάντα παρασχομένου.
ἀλλʼ ἐμὲ μηκέτʼ ἔχοιτε φίλοι φίλον, ἀλλʼ ἀπὸ πύργου
ῥίψατʼ, ἐπεὶ λίην Ἀστυάναξ γέγονα,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.13: ἰητροὺς εὗρόν ποτʼ ἐγὼ λείους δυσέρωτας,
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἰητροὺς εὗρόν ποτʼ ἐγὼ λείους δυσέρωτας,
τρίβοντας φυσικῆς φάρμακον ἀντιδότου.
οἱ δέ γε φωραθέντες, ἔχʼ ἡσυχίην ἐδέοντο·
κἀγὼ ἔφην σιγῶ, καὶ θεραπεύσετέ με.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.15: εἰ Γραφικοῦ πυγαῖα σανὶς δέδαχʼ ἐν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ Γραφικοῦ πυγαῖα σανὶς δέδαχʼ ἐν βαλανείῳ,
ἄνθρωπος τί πάθω; καὶ ξύλον αἰσθάνεται.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.16: μὴ κρύπτῃς τὸν ἔρωτα, Φιλόκρατες· αὐτὸς
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
μὴ κρύπτῃς τὸν ἔρωτα, Φιλόκρατες· αὐτὸς ὁ δαίμων
λακτίζειν κραδίην ἡμετέρην ἱκανός·
ἀλλʼ ἱλαροῦ μετάδος τι φιλήματος. ἔσθʼ ὅτε καὶ σὺ
αἰτήσεις τοιάνδʼ ἐξ ἑτέρων χάριτα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.21: Κλέψομεν ἄχρι τίνος τὰ φιλήματα, καὶ τὰ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.175: ἢ μὴ ζηλοτύπει δούλοις ἐπὶ παισὶν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἢ μὴ ζηλοτύπει δούλοις ἐπὶ παισὶν ἑταίρους,
ἢ μὴ θηλυπρεπεῖς οἰνοχόους πάρεχε.
τίς γὰρ ἀνὴρ ἐς ἔρωτʼ ἀδαμάντινος; ἢ τίς ἀτειρὴς
οἴνῳ; τίς δὲ καλοὺς οὐ περίεργα βλέπει;
ζώντων ἔργα τάδʼ ἐστὶν ὅπου δʼ οὐκ εἰσὶν ἔρωτες
οὐδὲ μέθαι, Διοφῶν, ἢν ἐθέλῃς, ἄπιθι·
κἀκεῖ Τειρεσίην ἢ Τάνταλον ἐς πότον ἕλκε,
τὸν μὲν ἐπʼ οὐδὲν ἰδεῖν, τὸν δʼ ἐπὶ μοῦνον ἰδεῖν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.176: στυγνὸς δὴ τί, Μένιππε, κατεσκέπασαι
poems.author: Strato of Sardis

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.178: Ἐξεφλέγην, ὅτε Θεῦδις ἐλάμπετο παισὶν ἐν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
Ἐξεφλέγην, ὅτε Θεῦδις ἐλάμπετο παισὶν ἐν ἄλλοις,
οἷος ἐπαντέλλων ἀστράσιν ἠέλιος,
τοὔνεκʼ ἔτι φλέγομαι καὶ νῦν, ὅτε νυκτὶ λαχνοῦται·
δυόμενος γάρ, ὅμως ἥλιός ἐστιν ἔτι.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.179: ὤμοσά σοι, Κρονίδη, μηπώποτε, μηδʼ ἐμοὶ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ὤμοσά σοι, Κρονίδη, μηπώποτε, μηδʼ ἐμοὶ αὐτῷ
ἐξειπεῖν ὅ τι μοι Θεῦδις ἔειπε λαβεῖν.
ψυχὴ δʼ ἡ δυσάπιστος ἀγαλλομένη πεπότηται
ἠέρι, καὶ στέξαι τἀγαθὸν οὐ δύναται·
ἀλλʼ ἐρέω, σύγγνωθι σύ μοι, Κεῖνος δὲ πέπεισται.
Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἀγνώστου τίς χάρις εὐτυχίης;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.180: καῦμὰ μʼ ἔχει μέγα δή τι· σὺ δʼ, ὦ παῖ,
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
καῦμὰ μʼ ἔχει μέγα δή τι· σὺ δʼ, ὦ παῖ, παύεο λεπτὸν
ἠέρι δινεύων ἐγγὺς ἐμεῖο λίνον.
ἄλλο τι πῦρ ἐμοῦ ἔνδον ἔχω κυάθοισιν ἀναφθέν,
καὶ περὶ σῇ ῥιπῇ μᾶλλον ἐγειρόμενον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.181: ψεύδεα μυθίζουσι, Θεόκλεες, ὡς ἀγαθαὶ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ψεύδεα μυθίζουσι, Θεόκλεες, ὡς ἀγαθαὶ μὲν
αἱ Χάριτες, τρισσαὶ δʼ εἰσὶ κατʼ Ὀρχομενὸν
πεντάκι γὰρ δέκα σεῖο περισκιρτῶσι πρόσωπα,
τοξοβόλοι, ψυχέων ἅρπαγες ἀλλοτρίων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.182: ταῦτά με νῦν τὰ περισσὰ φιλεῖς, ὅτʼ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ταῦτά με νῦν τὰ περισσὰ φιλεῖς, ὅτʼ ἔρωτος ἀπέσβη
πυρσός, ὅτʼ οὐδʼ ἄλλως ἡδὺν ἔχω σε φίλον.
μέμνημαι γὰρ ἐκεῖνα τὰ δύσμαχα· πλὴν ἔτι, Δάφνι,
ὀψὲ μέν, ἀλλʼ ἐχέτω καὶ μετάνοια τόπον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.183: τίς χάρις, Ἡλιόδωρε, φιλήμασιν, εἴ με
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
τίς χάρις, Ἡλιόδωρε, φιλήμασιν, εἴ με λάβροισιν
χείλεσι μὴ φιλέεις ἀντιβιαζόμενος,
ἀλλʼ ἐπʼ ἄκροις ἀσάλευτα μεμυκόσιν, οἷα κατʼ οἴκους
καὶ δίχα σοῦ με φιλεῖ πλάσμα τὸ κηρόχυτον;

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.184: μὴ σπεύσῃς Μενέδημον ἑλεῖν δόλῳ, ἀλλʼ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
μὴ σπεύσῃς Μενέδημον ἑλεῖν δόλῳ, ἀλλʼ ἐπίνευσον
ὀφρύσι, καὶ φανερῶς αὐτὸς ἐρεῖ· πρόαγε.
οὐ γὰρ ἀνάβλησις· φθάνει δέ τε καὶ τὸν ἄγοντα·
οὐδʼ ἀμάρης, ποταμοῦ δʼ ἐστὶν ἑτοιμότερος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.185: τοὺς σοβαροὺς τούτους καὶ τοὺς
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
τοὺς σοβαροὺς τούτους καὶ τοὺς περιπορφυροσήμους
παῖδας, ὅσους ἡμεῖς οὐ προσεφιέμεθα,
ὥσπερ σῦκα πέτραισιν ἐπʼ ἀκρολόφοισι πέπειρα
ἔσθουσιν γῦπες, Δίφιλε, καὶ κόρακες.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.186: ἄχρι τίνος ταύτην τὴν ὀφρύα τὴν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἄχρι τίνος ταύτην τὴν ὀφρύα τὴν ὑπέροπτον,
Μέντορ, τηρήσεις, μηδὲ τὸ χαῖρε λέγων,
ὡς μέλλων αἰῶνα μένειν νέος, ἢ διὰ παντὸς
ὀρχεῖσθαι πυρίχην; καὶ τὸ τέλος πρόβλεπε.
ἥξει σοι πώγων, κακὸν ἔσχατον, ἀλλὰ μέγιστον
καὶ τότʼ ἐπιγνώσῃ τί σπάνις ἐστὶ φίλων.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.187: πῶς ἀναγινώσκειν, Διονύσιε, παῖδα
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
πῶς ἀναγινώσκειν, Διονύσιε, παῖδα διδάξεις,
μηδὲ μετεκβῆναι φθόγγον ἐπιστάμενος;
ἐκ νήτης μετέβης οὕτως ταχὺς εἰς βαρύχορδον
φθόγγον, ἀπʼ ἰσχνοτάτης εἰς τάσιν ὀγκοτάτην.
πλὴν οὐ βασκαίνω· μελέτα μόνον ἀμφοτέρους δὲ
κρούων, τοῖς φθονεροῖς λάμβδα καὶ ἄλφα λέγε.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.188: εἴ σε φιλῶν ἀδικῶ καὶ τοῦτο δοκεῖς ὕβριν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἴ σε φιλῶν ἀδικῶ καὶ τοῦτο δοκεῖς ὕβριν εἶναι,
τὴν αὐτὴν κόλασιν καὶ σὺ φίλει με λαβών.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.189: τίς σε κατεστεφάνωσε ῥόδοις ὅλον; εἰ μὲν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
τίς σε κατεστεφάνωσε ῥόδοις ὅλον; εἰ μὲν ἐραστής,
ἆ μάκαρ· εἰ δʼ ὁ πατήρ, ὄμματα καὐτὸς ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.190: ὄλβιος ὁ γράψας σε, καὶ ὄλβιος οὗτος ὁ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ὄλβιος ὁ γράψας σε, καὶ ὄλβιος οὗτος ὁ κάλλει
τῷ σῷ νικᾶσθαι κηρὸς ἐπιστάμενος.
θριπὸς ἐγὼ καὶ σύρμα τερηδόνος εἴθε γενοίμην,
ὡς ἀναπηδήσας τὰ ξύλα ταῦτα φάγω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.191: οὐκ ἐχθὲς παῖς ἦσθα; καὶ οὐδʼ ὄναρ οὗτος
poems.author: Strato of Sardis

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.192: οὐ τέρπουσι κόμαι με, περισσότεροί τε
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
οὐ τέρπουσι κόμαι με, περισσότεροί τε κίκιννοι,
τέχνης, οὐ φύσεως ἔργα διδασκόμενοι·
ἀλλὰ παλαιστρίτου παιδὸς ῥύπος ὁ ψαφαρίτης,
καὶ χροιὴ μελέων σαρκὶ λιπαινομένη.
ἡδὺς ἀκαλλώπιστος ἐμὸς πόθος· ἡ δὲ γοῆτις
μορφὴ θηλυτέρης ἔργον ἔχει Παφίης.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.193: οὐδέ Σμυρναῖαι Νεμέσεις ὅ τι σοὶ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
οὐδέ Σμυρναῖαι Νεμέσεις ὅ τι σοὶ πιλέγουσιν,
Ἀρτεμίδωρε, νοεῖς· μηδὲν ὑπὲρ τὸ μέτρον.
ἀλλʼ οὕτως ὑπέροπτα καὶ ἄγρια κοὐδὲ πρέποντα
κωμῳδῷ φθέγγῃ, πάνθʼ ὑποκρινόμενος.
μνησθήσῃ τούτων, ὑπερήφανε· καὶ σὺ φιλήσεις,
καὶ κωμῳδήσεις τὴν Ἀποκλειομένην,

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.194: εἰ Ζεὺς ἐκ γαίης θνητοὺς ἔτι παῖδας ἐς
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ Ζεὺς ἐκ γαίης θνητοὺς ἔτι παῖδας ἐς αἴθρην
ἥρπαζεν, γλυκεροῦ νέκταρος οἰνοχόους,
αἰετὸς ἂν πτερύγεσσιν Ἀγρίππαν τὸν καλὸν ἡμῶν
ἤδη πρὸς μακάρων ἦγε διηκονίας.
ναὶ μὰ σὲ γάρ, Κρονίδη, κόσμου πάτερ, ἢν ἐσαθρήσῃς
τὸν Φρύγιον ψέξεις αὐτίκα Δαρδανίδην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.195: ἄνθεσιν οὐ τόσσοισι φιλοζέφυροι χλοάουσι
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἄνθεσιν οὐ τόσσοισι φιλοζέφυροι χλοάουσι
λειμῶνες, πυκιναῖς εἴαρος ἀγλαΐαις,
ὅσσους εὐγενέτας, Διονύσιε, παῖδας ἀθρήσεις,
χειρῶν Κυπρογενοῦς πλάσματα καὶ Χαρίτων.
ἔξοχα δʼ ἐν τούτοις Μιλήσιος ἠνίδε θάλλει,
ὡς ῥόδον εὐόδμοις λαμπόμενον πετάλοις.
ἀλλʼ οὐκ οἶδεν ἴσως, ἐκ καύματος ὡς καλὸν ἄνθος,
οὕτω τὴν ὥρην ἐκ τριχὸς ὀλλυμένην.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.196: ὀφθαλμοὺς σπινθῆρας ἔχεις, θεόμορφε
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ὀφθαλμοὺς σπινθῆρας ἔχεις, θεόμορφε Λυκῖνε,
μᾶλλον δʼ ἀκτῖνας, δέσποτα, πυρσοβόλους.
ἀντωπὸς βλέψαι βαιὸν χρόνον οὐ δύναμαί σοι·
οὕτως ἀστράπτεις ὄμμασιν ἀμφοτέροις.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.197: Καρὸν γνῶθι σοφῶν τῶν ἑπτά τις, εἶπε,
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
Καρὸν γνῶθι σοφῶν τῶν ἑπτά τις, εἶπε, Φίλιππε
πάντα γὰρ ἀκμάζοντʼ ἐστὶν ἐραστότερα·
καὶ σίκυος πρῶτός που; ἐπʼ ἀνδήροισιν ὁραθεὶς
τίμιος, εἶτα συῶν βρῶμα πεπαινόμενος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.198: ἡλικίης φίλος εἰμὶ καὶ οὐδένα παῖδα
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἡλικίης φίλος εἰμὶ καὶ οὐδένα παῖδα προτάσσω,
πρὸς τὸ καλὸν κρίνων ἄλλο γὰρ ἄλλος ἔχει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.199: ἄρκιον ἤδη μοι πόσιος μέτρον εὐσταθίη
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἄρκιον ἤδη μοι πόσιος μέτρον εὐσταθίη γὰρ
λύεται ἥ τε φρενῶν ἥ τε διὰ στόματος.
χὠ λύχνος ἔσχισται διδύμην φλόγα, καὶ δὶς ἀριθμέω,
πολλάκι πειράζων, τοὺς ἀνακεκλιμένους.
ἤδη δʼ οὐκέτι μοῦνον ἐπʼ οἰνοχόον σεσόβημαι,
ἀλλὰ πάρωρα βλέπω κἠπὶ τὸν ὑδροχόον.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.200: μισῶ δυσπερίληπτα φιλήματα, καὶ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
μισῶ δυσπερίληπτα φιλήματα, καὶ μαχιμώδεις
φωνάς, καὶ σθεναρὴν ἐκ χερὸς ἀντίθεσιν
καὶ μὴν καὶ τόν, ὅτʼ ἐστὶν ἐν ἀγκάσιν, εὐθὺ θέλοντα
καὶ παρέχοντα χύδην, οὐ πάνυ δή τι θέλω·
ἀλλὰ τὸν ἐκ τούτων ἀμφοῖν μέσον, οἷον ἐκεῖνον
τὸν καὶ μὴ παρέχειν εἰδότα καὶ παρέχειν.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.201: εἰ μὴ νῦν Κλεόνικος ἐλεύσεται, οὐκέτʼ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ μὴ νῦν Κλεόνικος ἐλεύσεται, οὐκέτʼ ἐκεῖνον
δέξομʼ ἐγὼ μελάθροις, οὐ μὰ τὸν — οὐκ ὀμόσω.
εἰ γὰρ ὄνειρον ἰδὼν οὐκ ἤλυθεν, εἶτα παρείη
αὔριον, οὐ παρὰ τὴν σήμερον ὀλλύμεθα.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.202: πτηνὸς Ἔρως ἄγαγέν με διʼ ἠέρος, ἡνίκα,
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
πτηνὸς Ἔρως ἄγαγέν με διʼ ἠέρος, ἡνίκα, Δᾶμι,
γράμμα σὸν εἶδον, ὅ μοι δεῦρο μολεῖν σ’ ἔλεγεν
ῥίμφα δʼ ἀπὸ Σμύρνης ἐπὶ Σάρδιας· ἔδραμεν ἄν μου
ὕστερον εἰ Ζήτης ἔτρεχεν, ἢ Κάλαϊς.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.203: οὐκ ἐθέλοντα φιλεῖς με, φιλῶ δʼ ἐγὼ οὐκ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
οὐκ ἐθέλοντα φιλεῖς με, φιλῶ δʼ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἐθέλοντα·
εὔκολος ἢν φεύγω, δύσκολος ἢν ἐπάγω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.204: χρύσεα χαλκείων νῦν εἴπατε· δὸς λάβε
poems.author: Strato of Sardis

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.205: παῖς τις ὅλως ἁπαλὸς τοῦ γείτονος οὐκ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
παῖς τις ὅλως ἁπαλὸς τοῦ γείτονος οὐκ ὀλίγως με
κνίζει· πρὸς τὸ θέλειν δʼ οὐκ ἀμύητα γελᾷ·
οὐ πλεῦν δʼ ἐστὶν ἐτῶν δύο καὶ δέκα. νῦν ἀφύλακτοι
ὄμφακες· ἢν δʼ ἀκμάσῃ, φρούρια καὶ σκόλοπες

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.206: α. ἢν τούτῳ † φωνῇς, τὸ μέσον λάβε, καὶ
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
α. ἢν τούτῳ † φωνῇς, τὸ μέσον λάβε, καὶ κατακλίνας
ζεύγνυε, καὶ πρώσας πρόσπεσε, καὶ κάτεχε.
β. οὐ φρονέεις, Διόφαντε· μόλις δύναμαι γὰρ ἔγωγε
ταῦτα ποιεῖν· παίδων δʼ ἡ πάλη ἔσθʼ ἑτέρα.
μοχλοῦ καὶ μένε, Κῦρι, καὶ ἐμβάλλοντος ἀνάσχου·
πρῶτον συμμελετᾶν ἢ μελετᾷν μαθέτω.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.207: ἐχθὲς λουόμενος Διοκλῆς ἀνενήνοχε σαύραν
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
ἐχθὲς λουόμενος Διοκλῆς ἀνενήνοχε σαύραν
ἐκ τῆς ἐμβάσεως τὴν Ἀναδυομένην.
ταύτην εἴ τις ἔδειξεν Ἀλεξάνδρῳ τότʼ ἐν Ἴδῃ,
τὰς τρεῖς ἂν ταύτης προκατέκρινε θεάς.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.208: εὐτυχές, οὐ φθονέω, βιβλίδιον ἦ ῥὰ σ’
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εὐτυχές, οὐ φθονέω, βιβλίδιον ἦ ῥὰ σ’ ἀναγνοὺς
παῖς τις ἀναθλίψει, πρὸς τὰ γένεια τιθείς·
ἢ τρυφεροῖς σφίγξει περὶ χείλεσιν, ἢ κατὰ μηρῶν
εἰλήσει δροσερῶν, ὦ μακαριστότατον
πολλάκι φοιτήσεις ὑποκόλπιον, ἢ παρὰ δίφρους
βληθὲν τολμήσεις κεῖνα θιγεῖν ἀφόβως.
πολλὰ δʼ ἐν ἠρεμίῃ προλαλήσεις· ἀλλʼ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν,
χαρτάριον, δέομαι, πυκνότερόν τι λάλει.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.209: μήτε λίην στυγνὸς παρακέκλισο, μήτε
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
μήτε λίην στυγνὸς παρακέκλισο, μήτε κατηφής,
Δίφιλε, μηδʼ εἴης παιδίον ἐξ ἀγέλης.
ἔστω που προύνικα φιλήματα, καὶ τὰ πρὸ ἔργων
παίγνια, πληκτισμοί, κνίσμα, φίλημα,˘ λόγος.

poems.title: Anthologia Graeca XII.211: εἰ μὲν ἔφυς ἀμύητος ἀκμὴν ὑπὲρ οὗ σ’ ἔτι
poems.author: Strato of Sardis
poems.text:
εἰ μὲν ἔφυς ἀμύητος ἀκμὴν ὑπὲρ οὗ σ’ ἔτι πείθω,
ὀρθῶς ἂν δείσαις, δεινὸν ἴσως δοκέων.
εἰ δέ σε δεσποτικὴ κοίτη πεποίηκε τεχνίτην,
τί φθονέεις δοῦναι, ταὐτὸ λαβὼν, ἑτέρῳ;
ὃς μὲν γὰρ καλέσας ἐπὶ τὸ χρέος, εἶτʼ ἀπολύσας,
εὕδει κύριος ὤν, μηδὲ λόγου μεταδούς·
ἄλλη δʼ ἔνθα τρυφή· παίξεις ἴσα, κοινὰ λαλήσεις,
τἆλλα δʼ ἐρωτηθεὶς κοὐκ ἐπιτασσόμενος.
